name: PostgreSQL
role: Backend engineers and database developers use PostgreSQL for structured application data, queries and durable invariants.
technical: Tables, SQL, foreign keys and transactions model related records. Indexes support access paths; concurrency and transaction isolation govern how concurrent work observes changes.
tradeoffs: Use constraints for durable rules, parameterized queries for values and explicit transaction boundaries. Inspect query plans and test backup restoration. CODARIS uses PostgreSQL through libpq from its native C backend.
exercise: Build a reading-list schema with unique and foreign-key constraints, then test a concurrent update.

name: SQLite
role: Application and device developers use SQLite when data should live with the application rather than behind a separate database server.
technical: An in-process SQL engine stores a database in a local file. Transactions and indexes remain useful even when there is no separate server process.
tradeoffs: Plan file ownership, backup and write contention. Embedded deployment changes operational boundaries; it does not make concurrent writes unlimited.
exercise: Build an offline catalogue and verify a rollback leaves no partial update.

name: MySQL
role: Backend and database teams use MySQL for SQL-based application storage and transactional workloads.
technical: The InnoDB storage engine provides transactions, row-level locking and foreign keys. SQL queries use indexes and an optimizer to select access paths.
tradeoffs: Review isolation, deadlocks and index choices. Treat migration locking and replication behavior as operational design decisions.
exercise: Model an order and its items with a transaction and test rollback on failure.

name: MongoDB
role: Application developers use MongoDB for data represented as documents with related values and nested structures.
technical: Documents can embed related data or reference other documents. Schema design follows access patterns; indexes support queries and validation can constrain stored shapes.
tradeoffs: Flexible schema still needs a data model. Weigh duplication and document growth against the cost of separate reads and cross-document updates.
exercise: Model a product catalogue and compare embedding variants with referencing them.

name: Redis
role: Backend and platform engineers use Redis for fast access to keys and data structures in workloads such as caching and coordination.
technical: Strings, hashes, lists, sets and other structures expose purpose-specific operations. Persistence, eviction and replication settings shape operational behavior.
tradeoffs: Decide whether data is authoritative or rebuildable. Define expiration, eviction and cache-miss behavior; do not assume every deployment has the same durability guarantees.
exercise: Build a bounded cache and test expiry, eviction and upstream failure.

name: Apache Cassandra
role: Distributed-systems teams use Cassandra for partitioned data and workloads designed around known access patterns.
technical: Partition keys distribute records; clustering organizes data within partitions. Replication and tunable consistency affect availability and read/write behavior.
tradeoffs: Design queries before tables and avoid unbounded hot partitions. Plan repairs, retention and failure testing rather than treating distribution as automatic reliability.
exercise: Design a time-bucketed event table and explain its partition-size bound.

name: Neo4j
role: Developers working with connected data use Neo4j to model relationships explicitly and traverse them.
technical: Nodes and relationships can carry properties; labels and relationship types express meaning. Graph queries follow patterns across connected records.
tradeoffs: Bound traversal depth and inspect query plans. Graph modelling is useful when relationships drive the queries; it does not remove indexing or transaction design.
exercise: Model projects, contributors and dependencies, then query a bounded dependency path.

name: Elasticsearch
role: Search and platform teams use Elasticsearch to retrieve and aggregate indexed documents.
technical: Search visibility is near-real-time: an indexed change may require a refresh before appearing in search results. Analysis and mappings influence how text is indexed.
tradeoffs: Design reindexing and source-of-truth recovery. Distinguish acknowledgement from search visibility and budget shard count, memory and storage.
exercise: Index a small document set and test the interval between a write and searchable results.

name: DuckDB
role: Analysts and data-tool developers use DuckDB for SQL analytics within an application or local workflow.
technical: An in-process analytical engine supports column-oriented execution and data-file workflows. Its role differs from a shared transactional application server.
tradeoffs: Test memory requirements and representative scans. Separate analytical access patterns from highly concurrent request-by-request updates.
exercise: Query a local dataset and compare a full scan with a filtered aggregation.

name: Amazon DynamoDB
role: Cloud application teams use DynamoDB for managed, partitioned application data with key-oriented access.
technical: Partition and sort keys shape access patterns. Secondary indexes add alternate query paths; throughput and consistency behavior depend on the operation and configuration.
tradeoffs: Avoid hot keys, understand index limitations and model cost under real traffic. Managed operation still requires access control, backup and failure planning.
exercise: Design keys for a tenant-scoped activity feed and test a heavily active tenant.

name: Qdrant
role: Search and machine-learning teams use Qdrant to retrieve vectors by similarity with associated payload filters.
technical: Collections organize points containing vectors and payload data. Similarity search depends on the embedding model, distance metric and index configuration.
tradeoffs: Measure recall and latency on representative queries. Enforce tenant filters and plan embedding-version migrations; similarity is not factual correctness.
exercise: Create a small semantic-search benchmark with labelled relevant results.

name: Supabase
role: Application teams use Supabase to combine a PostgreSQL database with platform services and developer-facing APIs.
technical: The database remains PostgreSQL, while the platform supplies additional integration surfaces. Engine capabilities and platform responsibilities are distinct layers.
tradeoffs: Design row-level access policies and keep privileged credentials on the server. Review backups, migrations and the trust boundary of every exposed API.
exercise: Create a tenant-owned table and test policies with two different users.
